title: Bermuda: 6 Planes Gone｜Curio Archive
description:
On December 5, 1945, five U.S. Navy training planes and one rescue plane, 27 men in all, vanished off Florida on the same night. Why did this one night become the most famous evidence for the "Bermuda Triangle"?
For anyone who likes tracing legends back to the original records.

This episode follows that afternoon in order: the radio calls, the flames seen after the rescue plane took off, the Navy's investigation report and its 1947 correction. Then we look at which year, and which article, made the name "Bermuda Triangle" famous. Finally, we look at how NOAA, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, answers the question: is that sea really more dangerous? Sources for every time and number are listed in the references below.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. The people and scenes shown are illustrative, not real photos.

t001.text: You know the Bermuda Triangle, between Florida, Bermuda and Puerto Rico.

t002.text: They say planes and ships vanish once they go in.

t003.text: Films and songs told its story.

t004.text: Yet its top evidence is a single afternoon.

t005.text: Winter 1945: five Navy planes never returned.

t006.text: Even their rescue plane never came back.

t007.text: And one radio line in between got quoted worldwide: don't come after me.

t008.text: So today: how did one afternoon become the devil's sea the world fears?

t011.text: At Naval Air Station Fort Lauderdale, Florida, trainees flew daily.

t012.text: Nineteenth in line that afternoon, it was Flight 19, a final navigation class.

t013.text: Think of it as a final driving test.

t014.text: They were Avenger torpedo bombers with 14 men.

t015.text: Some were 18; others were war veterans.

t017.text: Remember this: he'd moved from Miami just two weeks before, new to the area.

t018.text: Takeoff at 2:10 p.m. East to the Bahamas for bombing practice, then north, then back to base.

t019.text: When I first saw this route, I froze: it was itself a triangle.

t020.text: Due back in under three hours. So which turn went wrong?

t021.text: Around 3:45, a nearby instructor, Robert Cox, heard a student in his headset:

t023.text: Cox called them. Taylor said: "Both my compasses are out. I'm sure I'm in the Florida Keys."

t024.text: The Keys: the island chain at Florida's tip.

t025.text: Strange: an hour into that route, they couldn't be that far south.

t026.text: The base museum's director blames that earlier detail: newly arrived, he may have mistaken Bahamas islets for the Keys.

t027.text: Cox offered to come guide them. Taylor gave the opening line: No, I know where I am. Don't come after me.

t028.text: Remember it. Nearly 30 years on, someone would tack half a sentence onto it.

t029.text: Ground told them: fly west, toward the sun, and you'll hit Florida's coast.

t031.text: But Taylor's voice grew fainter. They were getting farther from shore, not closer.

t032.text: At 4:45, Taylor turned north to rule out being over the Gulf of Mexico.

t033.text: At 5:15 he seemed to figure it out: fly west until we hit the beach or run out of fuel.

t034.text: He said: stay close, ditch together.

t035.text: Here's the problem. Just after six, he said the crucial line: we didn't go far enough east, turn around, go east again.

t036.text: By now coastal airfields and ships had lights on to guide them home, but they flew the opposite way.

t037.text: Then ground got a rough fix: north of the Bahamas, at sea east of Daytona Beach.

t038.text: So why not send a plane out there?

t039.text: They did have one. A plane stood by, and once landed, Cox offered to take it out.

t040.text: The training flight officer said no. He later testified he was certain they'd make the coast before the fuel ran out.

t041.text: Darkness came; wind and waves rose.

t042.text: At 7:04, someone heard one pilot, Joseph Bossi, calling Taylor.

t043.text: No answer. It was the last word ever heard from the flight.

t045.text: At 7:27, the rescue from the start launched: two PBM Mariner flying boats.

t046.text: One carried 13 men. Less than half an hour after takeoff, it too vanished from the radio. Where did it go?

t047.text: At 7:50, a nearby merchant ship, Gaines Mills, saw flames shoot about 30 meters high off the water.

t049.text: Why would it burn? These planes had a nickname, 'the flying gas tank': lots of fuel, easy to ignite.

t050.text: And the men? Next came five days of the largest peacetime search yet.

t051.text: The Navy alone sent 248 aircraft and 18 ships.

t052.text: They searched over 200,000 square miles. By my math, that's about 14 Taiwans.

t053.text: Four days on, news said six rafts were found; officials soon called it a mistake.

t054.text: In the end: six planes, 27 men, not one confirmed piece of wreckage.

t055.text: How would the Navy explain this?

t056.text: In January, the Navy's report came out. It admitted the search coordination could improve.

t057.text: But the chief of naval air training was blunter: the leader's confusion bordered on some mental aberration.

t058.text: His mother, Katherine, got the telegram in class in Texas.

t059.text: She walked out and never taught again.

t060.text: She refused to believe it. No plane was found, and the pilot couldn't defend himself. Why pin it all on him?

t061.text: She went to Florida to grill the searchers.

t062.text: She wrote his 18-year-old radioman's mother too.

t063.text: The Navy's file on her? 'Emotionally unstable.'

t064.text: Think it ended there? Not yet.

t065.text: In 1947, after her persistent appeals, a Navy records board changed the finding:

t066.text: the flight was lost for 'causes unknown.'

t067.text: Those words meant something simple: without evidence, you can't blame Taylor.

t069.text: In 1950, the AP lumped together several plane and ship losses off the Southeast U.S.

t070.text: It also wrongly said the flight vanished in total radio silence.

t071.text: We just heard 3-plus hours of it!

t072.text: In 1964, Argosy, a men's magazine, ran Vincent Gaddis's 'The Deadly Bermuda Triangle.'

t073.text: Deadly Bermuda Triangle: the name caught on from this very Gaddis article.

t074.text: Weirder, he called them the Lost Patrol. Yet that navigation class from earlier was no patrol.

t075.text: In 1974, writer Charles Berlitz's book The Bermuda Triangle became a bestseller.

t076.text: His book adds to 'don't come after me': they look like they're from outer space.

t078.text: That rescue plane was blamed on the same force, though it was sent there to find them.

t079.text: And 'causes unknown' turned from a mother's vindication of her son into proof of a mysterious force.

t080.text: Back to our question. The U.S. agency NOAA is blunt: it's no official place name, and no official map draws its borders.

t081.text: And there's no evidence of more mysterious losses there than in other big, busy waters.

t082.text: Why the wrecks, then? Most Atlantic tropical storms and hurricanes cross here.

t083.text: Add the swift Gulf Stream, fickle weather and many shoals.

t084.text: Lots of ships, tough weather. Not a curse, I think.

t085.text: Back to that 1947 finding: it never said the sea took them.

t086.text: What we truly don't know is how he got lost, and what those young men went through after that 7:04 call.

t087.text: Less fun than aliens, but sadder.

t088.text: A question for you: if you were Cox that day and your superior said no, would you stay grounded, or fly out to search?

t090.text: If you like tracing legends back to the records, subscribe to Curio Archive. Okay, that's today's file.
